title: A Kitchen for the Songbook
premise: Paloma Crane has spent a decade keeping her late grandmother's lighthouse-turned-guesthouse on the Cornish coast, writing novels nobody reads and guarding a heart she broke herself at twenty-five. When a freak snowstorm strands rival winemakers Theo Marchetti and Jonah Vane — the two men who once loved her, and each other's best friends, until one catastrophic summer — under her roof, old truths about that mistake resurface alongside new ones about her grandmother's will, which leaves the guesthouse to whoever can prove they belong. As thaw turns to harvest season, Paloma must choose between the safe solitude she inherited and the messy, three-sided love that never actually ended; in the end, none of them wins the house alone — they keep it together, signing the deed as four names instead of one.
about_author: Zephyrine Eastwick is the pen name of a former pastry chef who spent six winters cooking in coastal guesthouses before turning to fiction full-time. She writes love stories where kitchens are confessional booths and second chances arrive unannounced, usually by storm.

chapters.title: The Last Train Before Winter
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. She closes the guesthouse for the season, notes the last train gone from the valley station, and finds her grandmother's will tucked in a recipe book — with a clause she doesn't understand. Emotional beat: comfortable loneliness cracked open by an inheritance that demands more than grief.

chapters.title: Two Coats on One Hook
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. A whiteout snowstorm brings two stranded travelers up the cliff path: Theo and Jonah, soaked, arguing, unmistakably the men from her past. She lets them in because no one freezes on her watch. Emotional beat: dread braided with a shameful flicker of joy.

chapters.title: Soup as Interrogation
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Over forced dinner, he watches Paloma pretend not to remember everything while feeding them like it's 2014. He catalogues what ten years changed — and what didn't. Emotional beat: nostalgia weaponized into tenderness he refuses to name.

chapters.title: The Mistake of Their Twenties
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. A power cut forces candles and confession: the night in the vineyard cellar that ended all three friendships is finally told from his side — including the part Paloma was never told. Emotional beat: guilt that has calcified into identity beginning to crack.

chapters.title: What Gran Knew
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Digging through her grandmother's letters, she discovers the will's 'belonging' clause was written after Gran met Theo and Jonah years ago. The house was always meant to be a test. Emotional beat: betrayal curdling into curiosity.

chapters.title: Snowed In, Walled Up
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Days of confinement compress old wounds: Theo and Jonah's rivalry over the vineyard deal that could ruin one of them, and their unfinished history with each other. Paloma referees from the kitchen doorway. Emotional beat: proximity making denial impossible.

chapters.title: Kiss Me Like the Road Is Open
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The roads clear; the trains run; nobody leaves. A near-kiss with Jonah in the pantry is interrupted by Theo — who doesn't object so much as join the silence. Emotional beat: want overriding a decade of self-protection.

chapters.title: Three Places Set
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He stays 'to help with winter repairs,' lying to himself about the vineyard crisis waiting for him downriver. A quiet scene fixing the guesthouse stove becomes a negotiation about who broke what. Emotional beat: loyalty to a dead friendship vs. living desire.

chapters.title: The Rival's Ledger
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. Business intrudes: Theo learns Jonah's family winery is failing and the merger Theo proposed would save it — or swallow it. He must decide whether to use that leverage. Emotional beat: ambition discovering it has a conscience.

chapters.title: Letters in the Flour Bin
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. More of Gran's letters reveal Gran once loved two people too, and chose neither, and regretted it in ink for forty years. Paloma recognizes her own future if she chooses safety again. Emotional beat: inheritance reframed as warning.

chapters.title: First Frost, First Fight
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The triangle detonates: Jonah accuses Theo of using the storm as strategy; Theo accuses Jonah of running from both of them twice. Paloma, caught between, says the unforgivable true thing. Emotional beat: love expressed as damage.

chapters.title: The Empty Third Chair
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Theo leaves for the vineyard. The house feels larger and colder than any snowstorm made it. Jonah stays but sleeps in the boathouse. Emotional beat: getting what you asked for and starving on it.

chapters.title: Manuscript, Unsent
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. He finds Paloma's unpublished novel — about three people and a lighthouse — and reads enough to understand she's been writing their ending for a decade, unable to live it. Emotional beat: being seen without consent, and choosing gentleness anyway.

chapters.title: Harvest Calls
chapters.summary: Theo's POV. At the vineyard, first harvest looms and Theo's board demands he finalize the hostile merger. His father's voice in his head versus Jonah's face in his memory. Emotional beat: succession as a cage with a gilded door.

chapters.title: The Clause, Decoded
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. With the solicitor's help, Paloma learns the will requires 'proof of belonging' — occupancy, care, and witness — before the spring deadline, and that Gran named all three of them as potential heirs. Emotional beat: terror of hope with paperwork attached.

chapters.title: Vinegar and Honey
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Jonah goes to the vineyard to confront Theo before the merger vote; Paloma follows, done with being the prize rather than a person. In the tasting room, the three of them say the whole truth of the cellar night at last. Emotional beat: truth as demolition and foundation at once.

chapters.title: Climax: The Vote and the Storm Surge
chapters.summary: All three POVs interwoven. The merger vote, a spring gale threatening the guesthouse, and the will's deadline collide in one night. Theo kills the merger to save Jonah's winery; Jonah and Paloma race the tide to secure the house; each chooses the others over the safe option. Emotional beat: sacrifice revealing what was actually wanted.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Salt-Damp
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. Morning after: the house stands, the vote failed, and the three of them sit in wreckage of schedules and certainties, awkwardly alive together. No resolutions yet — just tea and trembling honesty. Emotional beat: rawness before repair.

chapters.title: Proof of Belonging
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. They assemble evidence for the solicitor: receipts, photographs, a season of shared meals — and realize Gran's real proof was never documentary. It's whether they'd still be there when no one required it. Emotional beat: obligation transmuting into choice.

chapters.title: Four Names on a Deed
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV. The solicitor reads the final condition; the three sign together, not as heirs competing but as household. Paloma finishes her novel with a different ending than she wrote at twenty-five. Emotional beat: claiming a life she once only drafted.

chapters.title: First Harvest Comes In
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. Autumn: the vineyard thrives under joint stewardship, the guesthouse reopens, and the town adjusts its gossip to accommodate three names above one door. Small domestic scenes — arguments about jam, a shared bed negotiated honestly. Emotional beat: ordinary joy earned the hard way.

chapters.title: A Kitchen for the Songbook
chapters.summary: Paloma's POV, epilogue. One year on: a storm strands strangers at their door, and Paloma opens it without hesitation, Gran's songbook open on the kitchen counter where supper waits. She writes the last line of her novel and lives it simultaneously. Emotional beat: belonging no longer proven — simply practiced.
